My Work with Chris Lakin

Six months ago I tweeted I was ready to “whore myself out to Babylon"

Guy
Dec 14, 2025

1.

Six months ago I tweeted I was ready to “whore myself out to Babylon”. By that I meant I was ready to start working and get a job. The tweet was a long-shot: could I get a sweet gig making money online?

Turns out I could. A few people reached out and we started working together. Among them, Chris Lakin.

I hadn’t done this type of work before, but it served me well. For the first time in a long time I had a clear answer to the question of what it is that I do. “I’m a comms consultant”. If pressed further, “I help people with their short and medium-form communications”. And, if pressed even further, “I help people with Twitter and Substack.”

And the answer was true too, which is always a nice bonus.

2.

I wanna tell you more about this collaboration but I don’t know where to start. Maybe from the beginning? I guess the first thing I learned was just how much knowledge is private. I already sorta knew this to be true, I just didn’t believe it. I still very much am foraging the open internet for knowledge, but most of it is in places you only get to through personal connections. I know it but can’t believe it—that’s just how much it offends my sensibilities.

All of this to say: I was really impressed by Chris’ private knowledge system. It takes the form of a Discord server with 40 people on it that works like a decentralized exobrain. Which I know sounds so cringe, but I think is actually the right way of thinking about it. He’s very disciplined, using categories, channels, and threads inside of channels to keep each topic tidy, and using a tiny set of norms to keep others from making it into a mess.

The tiny set of norms.

Back when I first joined the main categories were posts, tweets, and graphics. This has since grown to include screenshot essays and

I started writing the previous line and realized that I’m running against the problem described in Seeing Like a State—it’s very hard to convey just what is so good about this Discord knowledge engine because it is mētis through and through: tacit, situational, and context-sensitive in a way that doesn’t lend itself to be written down clearly the way that episteme—explicit and explicitable knowledge—demands. “You had to be there.”

Episteme monotheists, who think episteme is the only valid form of knowledge, might be skeptic which is… fair enough. I can’t do for them much more than this: it’s really good. A really impressive knowledge production artifact. Trust me, bro.

Trust me, bro.

What else do I wanna tell you about it… Yea—as I strokethrough above a lot of the work was on blog posts, tweets, and graphs. This time starting from the end: I enjoy making graphs.

Or, before that, I guess part of what impressed me was just how much thought was going into stuff? Like, all my blog posts have taken 1 hour MAX, my tweets only as long as it takes to type them. Chris, in contrast, had been workshopping some of his essays for YEARS. Now, I knew people workshopped stuff: I’ve been added to gcs that are just for workshopping tweets, and that’s cool—I can respect treating things as a craft. There’s something aesthetic about treating something as a craft in proportion to how miniscule it is. I think that’s where the Japanese get a lot of their charm: the smaller the thing you treat as a craft the more it works as an honest signal of your being a craftsman. Everyone can treat large things as a craft but it takes a Japanese twitterati craftsman to treat the very smallest.

Which brings us back to graphs. This is the kind of graph we’d workshop together:

Feeling an emotion as gradient descent on prediction error

Chris has a background in Machine Learning and so do a lot of his clients. Because of that they care about having things explained that way. I don’t, but with the infinite translational power of ChatGPT at my fingertips, I might as well. I enjoyed crafting these graphs, though I now think that’s over, given NanoBanana.

Like good craftsmen we spent a lot of time workshopping tweets. My enduring prolificity (~50 tweets/day for 5 years now!) has taught me… mētis: show me a tweet and I can tell you how to make it better and maybe even what is generating those point improvements. But I can’t just give a recipe (episteme) to make a good tweet. Hill-climbing, not specification, or so tells me Chat.

I consider my work here done as well, as Chris can now reliably express his thoughts through the medium of bangers.

Finally, the essays. Those were the most fun for me. Because I’ve always written them in one hour or less I never spent any time editing. Here I was exclusively editing. This made me realize that, if I were to train writing as a skill, that’s where I should’ve started.

You should start from the end. Gain the skill to finish something that is 99% done, then 98% done, then 97% done, etc. Working your way backwards from the end. I think the default is to start working forwards but then you hit a snag or motivation drops or it’s more complex than you anticipated and you end up leaving things unfinished, never getting the positive feedback that comes from completion. Yes, if I were to deliberately train writing as a skill I should start by editing others’ work, and only after editing, and drafting, my own. Work backwards and start from the end.

This to say I found editing very instructive. I found fighting with Chris in the Google Docs comments very instructive as his intuitions are the exact opposite of mine: he wants to be succinct to a fault, burning down all inferential bridges; I’m exhaustive to a fault, sprawling, obviously.

We had calls to debate the phrasing of a single sentence—which is so fun if you’re into writing, which is to say, if you’re into conveying your thoughts through writing—and he’d often use this heuristic that I love and have since tried and failed to adopt: “The best sentence is no sentence.” When in doubt, cut it out. A needed corrective to my (writing) character flaw.

I’ve been focusing on what working together was like from a procedural point of view. This makes sense. As the quote goes ”When art critics get together, they talk about form and structure and meaning. When artists get together, they talk about where you can buy cheap turpentine”.

Having said that, I also did learn a lot about Chris as a person, and about his philosophy. Like, the dude is the real deal, him being secure makes him real easy to work with compared to people who… aren’t. He takes setbacks in stride, is adaptable/flexible, and willing to negotiate. A pleasure to work with. Learning his philosophy also highlighted a number of mistakes I was making around the epistemics of inner work1. (The name of another Discord channel.)

The remainder of our collaboration was odds-and-ends. The 80% that make up the final 20%. Things like vibe checks—ensuring he was getting himself across online as well as irl—, workshopping his positioning away from negative-valenced “insecurity” and towards neutral-to-positive-valenced “unlearning”, getting his handle changed from @ChrisChipMonk to @Chrislakin, and a bunch more stuff like that.

Babylon was a success.

3.

Contrasting how Chris does things and how I do them made for a stark difference: I famously try to do everything on my own, no matter how much others push me to collab; I don’t work on things over time, being all about volume and energy; and I do it all out in the open. Participating in a different way of doing knowledge work—collaboratively, through time, with precision, and private workshopping—taught me something about what is possible and what must be going on behind the public knowledge front-end.

Six months ago I went to Babylon for a paycheck; instead I found a craft, and a friend to practice it with.

1

Yea, “epistemics of inner work” is really vague, even with the mētis excuse, so here’s an example: lots of people tell you to “just feel your feelings”. They’re not wrong to do so. Feeling your feelings is great, and very helpful. But it’s a bit retarded (my words) to use it as advice. Here’s why:

Who will be on the receiving end of this advice? It’s either people who are already doing it, for whom it’s useless, or people who are not. For the second group it begs the question: why aren’t they already feeling their feelings?

Sure, for a minority it’ll be because they hadn’t heard of it or thought of it before. It’ll be useful for those. But for the vast majority of people who hear it it’ll be because they can’t. The same way telling men that can’t get themselves to cry to just cry is less than helpful. There’s a reason they’re blocked on it. Maybe a bad reason, but maybe a good one! You don’t know.

The point is this: “Just feel your feelings” will be good advice exclusively for the set of people who (1) can do it, (2) for whom it’s good to do it and (3) who haven’t done it yet. I suggest this is a small but very vocal subset of people. You’re telling someone who just ran the whole marathon on their own to “Just get across the finish line”. You’re telling them to have the last bite that finally makes them satisfied. Of course they’ll be vocal: “Why doesn’t everyone just eat the last bite first?” Yea, but that’s not how it works…

That’s an example of the kind of stuff we’d discuss and workshop in that channel in particular

Well written.

The problem in the footnote is something I've been thinking about lately in different contexts. I've been toying with the idea that the reason people can't 'feel their feelings' when you tell them to is because those words don't actually mean for them what you are trying to tell them. (I'm inspired by 1 hr of reading Vygotsky, and some independent thinking).

It might not be a psychological block (it might be), just that they don't have this concept. And they need to be exposed to this concept in order to try it. For a select minority, they just never heard about 'feelings' as a good or useful thing. But for most people the act doesn't even exist as a category.

And for them, using physical sensation noticing, and showing how this is useful for gathering information about oneself, might be all that's needed. I'm only assuming they can understand 'notice sensations in your body' and then bridging it to emotions is something people can do. (does not seem crazy at all). And then using that as a way to answer questiosn like 'how do I feel right now' becomes 'sensation x, metaphor y, points towards emotion z' and using that information for themselves.

if once you teach people this, they only know how to notice their emotions in order to quash them, maybe you have a real psychological block. But i'd hazard 80% would just start using this like all the focusing folks.
